candidates.title: Laxative treatment perturbs gut microbiome composition and metabolism in humans independent of short-term fiber consumption: a randomized controlled crossover intervention study.
candidates.abstract: Gastrointestinal transit time is a major ecological determinant of the human gut microbiome, yet causal evidence that disentangles the effects of diet from those of the gut environment remains limited. Here, we conducted a randomized, controlled crossover trial in healthy adults (nine females, four males) consuming fully standardized high-fiber (40 g/d) or low-fiber (10 g/d) diets to assess how manipulating the gut environment using an osmotic laxative (Movicol) affects gut microbial composition and metabolism. Contrary to our hypothesis, laxative treatment did not affect the saccharolytic-to-proteolytic ratio. Yet, it induced a pronounced microbiome perturbation, explaining 16.3% of the variation in microbial community structure, compared with 1.7% explained by diet. The laxative treatment reduced the absolute abundance of several gram-positive commensals, including butyrate-producing taxa, while increasing gram-negative genera such as Bacteroides, Alistipes, and Phocaeicola. Our findings identify perturbations to the gut environment as a prominent short-term driver of human gut microbiome structure, independent of short-term fiber intake. Together, these results challenge a diet-centric view of microbiome modulation and raise concerns about potential detrimental effects on the gut microbiome in chronic use of gut environment-altering drugs such as macrogol-based laxatives.

candidates.title: The gut‒kidney axis.
candidates.abstract: Gut-kidney dialog is integral to the holobiont. This review explores the interactions between these two organ-systems across physicochemical, endocrine, immune, and metabolic levels. It is argued that the gut makes physiological concessions favoring the microbiota, which must be assured by the kidneys, extending the concept of renal homeostasis to holostasis. When considering pathological situations, three dimensions of the gut‒kidney axis are identified: (1) the gut causing kidney disease, (2) the effect of renal failure on the gut, and (3) the systemic effects of the gut in renal failure. Causal roles of the gut in enteric hyperoxaluria, IgA nephropathy and diabetic nephropathy are described. The impact of a uremic environment on the gut is discussed. Conversely the intestinal origins of uremic toxins and their impact on distant organs, including the kidneys themselves, are outlined. Special consideration is given to host-microbiota immune interactions, immunosuppressive therapy and kidney transplantation. Therapeutic interventions targeting the gut-kidney axis are appraised.

candidates.title: Microbiota-Bile acid decoupling contributes to altered postnatal growth and metabolism in sFGR: a twin-paired dynamic study with FMT validation.
candidates.abstract: Selective fetal growth restriction (sFGR) increases the risk of adverse long-term metabolic outcomes, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Bile acids (BAs) mediate gut microbiota-host metabolic crosstalk, and their early-life perturbation may underlie sFGR-associated health risks. Using a monochorionic diamniotic twin cohort (25 concordant pairs, 22 sFGR pairs), we developed a twin-specific analytical framework integrating birth weight deviation, intra-pair difference, and time-weighted variables. Through metagenomics, 16S rRNA sequencing, metabolomics, and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), we characterized gut microbiota colonization dynamics in sFGR neonates. Within 24 hours of birth, smaller twins (sFGR-S) exhibited gut microbiota "structure-function decoupling"-increased species diversity but decreased functional diversity-with markedly reduced abundance of Enterococcus faecium and bile salt hydrolase (BSH) genes. Under high peripheral BA pressure, the sFGR-S microbiota followed a three-stage trajectory: initial compensatory BSH enrichment, reversal within 72 hours following environmental microbial invasion, and subsequent functional collapse, with progressive dysbiosis that leads to metabolic dyshomeostasis. FMT demonstrated that sFGR-S microbiota was associated with gut-liver axis disruption, hydrophobic BA accumulation (LCA, DCA), intestinal barrier impairment, and chronic low-grade inflammation, suggesting a potential link between early "microbiota-BA" axis dysregulation and persistent metabolic disorders. These findings elucidate the mechanistic basis of sFGR-associated long-term risks, identify a postnatal "golden window" for intervention, and highlight BSH enzymatic activity and resistance to pathogenic colonization as key functional targets for improving postnatal growth and metabolic health.

candidates.title: Crop diversification promotes soil microbial carbon turnover.
candidates.abstract: Agricultural diversification alters plant residue chemistry and rhizodeposition, with legacy effects on soil organic matter (SOM) cycling. The priming effect (PE) and necromass formation are key processes of SOM dynamics, yet how diversification affects these processes, and SOM persistence remains poorly understood. Using 13C-labelled glucose in a 150-day incubation of soils (0-15 cm) from two contrasting diversification trials (43 and 8 years), we found that diversification increased SOM priming by 153-174% and retention of glucose-derived 13C in microbial necromass by 227-289%. Diversified soils also had more bioavailable C, dissolved organic C, and neutral sugars, stronger stoichiometric nutrient limitation (103% higher C:P imbalance and 15% lower vector angle), and higher microbial activity and N- and P-acquiring enzyme activities. Microbial C use efficiency increased by 65%, while replacing the native microbial community of diversified soils with that of conventional soils reduced CUE by 9% and 45% at the 43- and 8-year sites, respectively. Community-level analyses further linked greater retention of glucose-derived 13C in microbial necromass to putative Discosea and Bacillota co-occurrence patterns. Metagenomic profiling revealed 18-125% higher relative abundances of CAZyme genes involved in degrading plant- and microbial-derived compounds, alongside a modest (~4%) increase in Y-associated functional potential at both sites. Although priming-induced native-C losses exceeded the amount of glucose-derived 13C retained in microbial necromass, the ratio of necromass C retention to priming-induced C loss was 28% higher under diversification than under conventional cropping over the 150-day incubation. Crop diversification thus reshapes microbial C cycling, coupling enhanced native SOM mineralization with greater retention of added C in microbial necromass, making the net effect on SOC dependent on sustained C inputs.

candidates.title: Non-enzymatic assimilation of organosulfur compounds at the interface of geochemistry and biochemistry.
candidates.abstract: Dimethyl sulfide (DMS) and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) have important microbial-driven roles in global nutrient cycling, chemotaxis and/or climate regulation. Microbial DMSO and DMS assimilation were thought to require their enzymatic reduction to methanethiol. However, reactive oxygen species were recently shown to mediate methane production from DMS and DMSO. Here, we show that this oxidative mechanism can sustain microbial growth without the need for enzymes to directly reduce DMS or oxidize DMSO. In an interplay with iron, both light and heat were effective geochemical drivers of this mechanism that yielded methanesulfonic acid and sulfite, and which mimicked the stepwise oxidation of DMSO by monooxygenases that only enzymatically enhance this oxidation reaction. Furthermore, we demonstrated intracellular DMSO degradation, in which sulfur and the simultaneously released carbon were both utilized by microbes. This study emphasizes that metabolic pathways are not necessarily enzyme-driven, with putatively ancient, non-enzymatic reaction networks taking place at a transition between geochemistry and biochemistry.

candidates.title: Antibiotic effects on gut-derived short chain fatty acid pools in healthy volunteers.
candidates.abstract: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are vital microbial metabolites that maintain gut health and immune function. Despite the established deleterious effect of antibiotics on anaerobic bacteria in the gut, the longitudinal effects of antibiotics on SCFA pool dynamics remain poorly characterized in humans. This study aimed to characterize depletion and recovery of linear and branched SCFAs and to explore microbial taxa associated with changes to SCFA pools after antibiotic exposure. This was a secondary analysis of a phase 1, randomized, nonblinded clinical trial in young healthy volunteers given a 10-day course of oral vancomycin, omadacycline, or moxifloxacin. Fecal samples were collected at baseline, during antibiotics, and follow-up visits for SCFA determinations and amplicon-based microbiome characterizations. Mixed effects models demonstrated that vancomycin produced global suppression of SCFAs pool relative to baseline, indicating broad suppression of microbial fermentation. Although all antibiotics reduced SCFA levels during treatment, vancomycin associated changes were most evident for branched SCFAs vs. comparators. Vancomycin shifted the fermentation balance by disproportionately suppressing linear SCFAs, reflected by a lower linear-to-branched SCFA ratio. In parallel, Clostridiales abundance declined most markedly after vancomycin, with more moderate reductions after omadacycline and moxifloxacin. Moxifloxacin and omadacycline but not vancomycin showed early recovery of butyrate-production capacity by qPCR. In this longitudinal analysis of healthy volunteers, vancomycin caused global suppression of microbial fermentation, with marked depletion of linear and branched SCFAs consistent with disproportionate suppression of fiber fermentation relative to amino acid fermentation.

candidates.title: Fecal microbiota transplantation for pediatric Clostridioides difficile infection: efficacy, challenges, and the path to next-generation microbiome therapies.
candidates.abstract: Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is an increasing cause of morbidity in children, with recurrent disease posing substantial therapeutic challenges. Antibiotic therapy remains the cornerstone of initial management; however, up to 30% of children experience recurrence, and those with underlying comorbidities face recurrence rates as high as 65%. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) has demonstrated superior efficacy over antibiotics for recurrent CDI (rCDI) in adults and has emerged as the most effective available intervention for pediatric rCDI. In this review, we synthesize current evidence on FMT efficacy, microbiome changes, and safety in children with CDI. Data from large multicenter cohort studies demonstrate cure rates exceeding 80%, with comparable efficacy observed in high-risk subpopulations, including those with inflammatory bowel disease and immunocompromising conditions. Critical research gaps remain, including the absence of randomized controlled trials and limited long-term safety data in children. Despite demonstrated effectiveness, significant barriers limit FMT accessibility for children. The COVID-19 pandemic has substantially impacted availability, and current regulatory changes have further restricted access. The lack of FDA-approved live biotherapeutic products approved for CDI in children creates additional challenges. We critically examine the emerging pipeline of next-generation microbiome-based therapies and identify the steps required to ensure children with recurrent CDI have access to safe, effective, and approved treatments.
candidates.article_body_excerpt:
[Background]
Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is one of the leading healthcare-associated infections, with incidence rising over recent decades in both adults and children and an increasing shift toward community acquisition. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) has transformed the management of recurrent CDI (rCDI) in adults and demonstrated superiority over standard antibiotic therapy in randomized controlled trials (RCTs). 1 , 2 These compelling outcomes have prompted exploration of FMT in children with rCDI, where up to 30% of patients fail standard antibiotic therapy, and those with underlying conditions face recurrence rates as high as 65%. 3 Large observational studies have demonstrated FMT cure rates exceeding 80% in pediatric rCDI. However, recent restrictions on FMT access and the absence of approved microbiome-based live biotherapeutic products (LBPs) for patients under 18 have created a significant unmet need in children with recurrent and refractory disease. In this review, we discuss the rationale and efficacy of FMT for CDI in children, and critically examine the challenges – regulatory, biological, and therapeutic – that must be overcome to translate these findings into accessible, approved treatments for pediatric patients (Graphical abstract). This narrative review was conducted through a systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from inception through April 2026. The search terms included combinations of: “Clostridioides difficile,” “Clostridium difficile,” “CDI,” “fecal microbiota transplantation,” “FMT,” “live biotherapeutic product,” “pediatric,” “children,” and “recurrent.” Reference lists of identified articles were reviewed for additional relevant studies. The inclusion criteria encompassed clinical trials, cohort studies, case series, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and guidelines pertaining to pediatric CDI or FMT in children. Studies exclusively in adults were included where pediatric data were absent or to provide contextual comparison.

[Clostridioides difficile infection in children]
Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) is a gram-positive anaerobic bacterium that produces highly resistant spores that are transmitted via the fecal-oral route and can persist in healthcare and community environments, leading to widespread infections. 4 , 5 CDI produces a wide clinical spectrum ranging from mild diarrhea to severe hemorrhagic colitis, with potentially life-threatening complications, including toxic megacolon and death. 4 , 6 Antibiotic use, increasing age, and underlying comorbidities that promote gut dysbiosis all heighten susceptibility.
CDI rates rose dramatically from the 1990s in both adults and children, emerging as a global public health threat. 7 CDI was initially considered a predominantly healthcare associated (HA) illness, however a large U.S. study demonstrated a significant decrease from 7.09 HA-CDI pediatric cases per 10,000 patient days in 2013 to 4.89 cases per 10,000 patient-days in 2019 while community acquired (CA) CDI rates increased from 9.6/100,000 children per year in 2012 to peak at 16.9/100,000 children per year in 2015. 8 , 9 Subsequently, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Emerging Infections Program confirmed that the incidence of CA-CDI surpassed HA-CDI across all age groups, including children ages 1–17 y old where the incidence of CA-CDI is 21/100,000 persons and HA-CDI is 8.1/100,000 persons. 10 This shift likely reflects the adoption of robust infection control and antimicrobial stewardship measures in healthcare settings. 11 , 12
The most common risk factor for CDI in children is antibiotic exposure, particularly with clindamycin, third-generation cephalosporins, and fluoroquinolones. 13 , 14 Although most children with CDI report antibiotic exposure in the preceding 4 weeks, many have no prior antibiotic exposure, especially among those with CA-CDI. 15 Additionally, multiple courses of antibiotics further increase the risk of CDI (OR 1.93, 95% CI 1.25–2.97). 16 Acid suppressants, specifically proton pump inhibitors, also increase CDI risk, likely through their effects on the gut microbiome. 14 , 16 , 17 Prior hospitalization, length of hospitalization, and even recent outpatient visits are additional risk factors, underscoring the ongoing importance of infection control in pediatric settings. 14 Approximately 30%–50% of children who develop CDI have significant underlying comorbidities, including prior solid organ transplantation, immunodeficiency, malignancy, and inflammatory bowel d

[Current non-FMT treatment options]
The first step in management, regardless of the therapeutic agent being used, is discontinuation of the inciting antibiotic when able. Pediatric treatment guidelines from 2017 recommend that first-line antibiotic therapy for non-severe initial CDI or first recurrence in children includes oral metronidazole (7.5 mg/kg/dose three or four times daily for 10 d) or oral vancomycin (10 mg/kg/dose four times daily for 10 d). 34 A systematic review and meta-analysis of pediatric observational studies demonstrated significantly lower cure rates with metronidazole compared to vancomycin, consistent with adult data, and has driven increasing use of vancomycin in pediatric practice. 8 , 43 Metronidazole has been progressively de-prioritized in both adult and pediatric practice owing to inferior efficacy, increasing clinical failure rates, and palatability challenges from its metallic taste; its use is now generally discouraged except where access to alternatives is limited. For severe initial CDI, oral or rectal vancomycin, with or without intravenous metronidazole (10 mg/kg/dose three times daily), is recommended. For second or subsequent recurrences, recommended regimens include a tapered and pulsed vancomycin course over at least 6 weeks or vancomycin for 10 d followed by rifaximin for 20 d, with FMT as an alternative. 34 A shared limitation of these regimens is their frequent dosing, which has been consistently associated with reduced medication adherence. 44
While the 2021 adult CDI guidelines recommend fidaxomicin as first-line therapy for initial or rCDI, the pediatric IDSA/SHEA guidelines, last updated in 2017, do not yet reflect this recommendation. 34 , 45 However, compelling pediatric data exist. The SUNSHINE trial, a phase 3, multicenter RCT, compared fidaxomicin (oral suspension 16 mg/kg/dose twice daily for children under 6 y, or 200 mg tablets twice daily for older children) to vancomycin for 10 d in patients under 18 y of age. 46 Fidaxomicin demonstrated significantly higher rates of global cure, i.e., confirmed clinical response without rCDI until the time of assessment. A real-world, retrospective pediatric multicenter study supports these findings, showing that fidaxomicin is well-tolerated with a 78.5% cure rate without relapse at day 60. 47 Fidaxomicin’s twice-daily dosing and lower rCDI rate also make it an appealing option. Extended-pulsed fidaxomicin (EPFX) – administered twice daily for 5 d followed by every-other-day dosing for 20 d – has dem

[Rationale for FMT in pediatric CDI]
Gut dysbiosis plays a central role in CDI pathogenesis. Disruption of the commensal gut microbiota, most commonly by antibiotic exposure, permits CD colonization, proliferation, and toxin production. Despite a small number of effective treatments, rCDI is a common challenge in children, necessitating the need for FMT. 37-40
FMT is defined as the transfer of fecal material from a healthy screened donor into a patient with rCDI, with the goal of restoring microbial diversity and re-establishing colonization resistance against CD. 57 While the exact mechanism of clearance of C. difficile through FMT remains unclear, observed microbiome changes include: (1) relative increase in abundance of Bacteroidetes and decreased abundance of Proteobacteria; (2) increased diversity of the microbial communities; (3) post-FMT similarities between the patients’ microbiome and the donor flora; and (4) restoration of normal fecal bile acid composition. 58-60 FMT is now considered the standard of care for patients with rCDI non-responsive to antibiotics. 61
FMT was first described in the English literature in 1958 in adults with pseudomembranous enterocolitis. 62 The landmark RCT by van Nood et al. in 2013 demonstrated FMT superiority over vancomycin for rCDI (81% vs. 31% cure rate), 59 and numerous subsequent RCTs, observational studies, and registry data have confirmed FMT efficacy in adults with cure rates exceeding 90%. 1 , 63-67 The first reported pediatric FMT via nasogastric tube was in 2010, and the first colonoscopic FMT in a child was in 2012. 68 , 69
FMT for Recurrent CDI: The primary and best-evidenced indication for FMT in children is prevention of further episodes in those with rCDI – defined as two or more recurrences after an initial treated episode. The rationale is the restoration of gut microbial diversity and colonization resistance, disrupted by repeated antibiotic courses as per adults. Large pediatric cohorts confirm cure rates exceeding 80% for this indication, as discussed in detail below. 3 RCTs are not available in children.
FMT for severe, fulminant, or refractory CDI: FMT has also been used as rescue therapy in children with severe or fulminant CDI unresponsive to antibiotics, or in those with refractory disease. Evidence for this indication in children is limited to case reports and small series. 70 The physiologic rationale –rapid microbiome reconstitution to interrupt toxin-mediated colonic injury and potentially the immune-modulating effect of F

[Effectiveness and safety of FMT in pediatric CDI]
To date, no prospective RCTs have evaluated the use of FMT in children with CDI, representing a significant gap in the evidence base. Current evidence is limited to retrospective studies and single-center cohort studies (Table 1).

candidates.title: A specialized microbiome enriched in nitrification and halogen cycling potential resolved from multi-omics investigation of a Caribbean suboxic and acidic marine sinkhole.
candidates.abstract: Background The Luymes Sinkholes, located on the Luymes Bank northwest of Saba, represent a unique marine environment characterized by distinct biogeochemical gradients. Most noticeable is an acidic (pH ≈ 6.25) and suboxic (O2 Results We identified a distinct microbial community within the submerged acid lake different from the non-acidic sinkholes, with increased abundances of Nitrospinota, Thermoproteota, Planctomycetota, and Actinobacteriota. We also found three enriched classes of dissolved compounds within the submerged acid lake: (1) large, (2) low-polarity, and (3) halogenated metabolites, including iodides and halobenzoic acids. Correlations between microbial taxa and metabolite classes show potential links between nitrifying archaea and halogenated compound cycling. We further supported these findings using the functional annotation of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) and protein clusters showing enrichment of nitrification and halogen cycling genes, suggesting the presence of specialized degradation and biosynthetic pathways, directly connecting microbial metabolism to the observed geochemical conditions. Conclusion These findings demonstrate that the submerged acid lake contains specific microbially driven biogeochemical processes under acidified and low-oxygen conditions, providing a natural model for future extreme ocean acidification scenarios. With this multi‑omics approach, we were able to connect the microbial metabolism with this unique environment, thereby expanding our understanding of how both are interconnected. Video Abstract.
authors: do Canto Brum de Menezes Pena MM
candidates.article_body_excerpt:
[Introduction]
Across all environments, microbes help sustain ecosystems by exchanging and transforming key elements such as nitrogen [31], carbon, and sulfur [65, 73], generating energy through chemo- or phototrophic metabolisms, and recycling nutrients. Consequently, microbes directly shape their environments by altering nutrient availability, and the composition and redox structure of the Dissolved Organic Matter (DOM) comprising the exometabolome [45, 67, 77]. In turn, microbial community composition and function are shaped by physicochemical conditions, including pH, oxygen availability, nutrient supply, and hydrodynamic connectivity [69], leading to a bidirectional relationship where each impacts the other. Comprehensive multi-omics studies, integrating metagenomics, metabolomics, and environmental measurements, are needed to resolve the intricate biogeochemical connections that shape the microbiome [31, 57, 79, 81]. Such multi-omics studies have been made possible the development of untargeted high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry of metabolomes [11] with advanced data processing tools [15, 27] and high-throughput metagenome shotgun sequencing [36, 38, 58] followed by de novo assembly and functional annotation [70]. These advances allow for increasingly detailed characterizations of potential microbe-metabolite interactions [42]. Despite these technological advances, the application of fully integrated multi-omics approaches in natural systems remains limited as the high complexity and natural variability of these systems introduce challenges that are largely absent from laboratory-based experiments [59]. Naturally stratified or physically isolated systems provide valuable opportunities to overcome some of these challenges by offering stable gradients over relatively small spatial scales [26]. Marine sinkholes can thus function as natural laboratories, as they often host sharp biogeochemical transitions.
Here, we characterize the microbial ecology of the northern sinkholes in the Luymes Bank, located at the northeast margin of the Saba Bank in the Caribbean Sea. Several of these sinkholes were previously described by Humphreys et al. [30], characterizing their complex geological origins and physical structure. Notably, Humphreys et al. [30] described an acidic (pH ≈ 6.25) and suboxic (O2 < 60 µmol/kg) submerged ‘lake’ starting at a depth of 220 m within the sinkhole with the deepest bottom depth (306 m). This unusual environment is thought to originate from the

[Methods]
We collected a total of 59 paired metagenomic and metabolomic samples from 21 stations on the Luymes Bank near Saba in December 2019 (Fig. 1A). Water chemistry parameters were measured as described by [30] (Supplementary Methods, Supplementary Table S3). Based on these parameters samples were clustered using Ward’s minimal variance clustering into six environments as follows: surface (n = 16), platform (n = 12), shallow sinkhole (n = 14), deep sinkhole (n = 9), acid lake (n = 6), and mesopelagic (n = 2). More detailed information on sample collection and storage can be found in the Supplementary methods.
Characterization of the environment: A map of Luymes Bank and integrated sinkholes (modified from Humphreys et al. 2022). B Ward’s minimal variance clustering of physicochemical parameters; rows correspond to samples and are annotated by the six defined environmental clusters (surface (n = 16), platform (n = 12), shallow sinkhole (n = 14), deep sinkhole (n = 9), acid lake (n = 6), and mesopelagic (n = 2)). Before clustering all nutrients were log10 transformed and all factors were normalized using z-scores. C Sampling depths of samples grouped by sinkhole and area (FS = far south, E = east, S = south, W = west, N = north, and O = open ocean). Colored by environmental cluster, see B. D Boxplots of measured physicochemical parameters grouped and colored by environmental cluster, see legend in B
Flow cytometric enumeration of prokaryotes (including bacteria and archaea) and viruses was performed at the NIOZ according to the protocol by Brussaard et al. [6] and using a TE buffer at pH 8.2. Samples were diluted in TE buffer and stained with the nucleic acid-specific green fluorescence dye SYBRGreen-I (10–5 dilution of commercial stock, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) for 15 min at room temperature for prokaryotes and for 10 min at 80 °C for viruses. Samples were then analyzed using a FACSCalibur flow cytometer with a 488 nm laser (BD Biosciences, USA).
Total DNA was extracted from seawater using the NucleoSpin Tissue DNA extraction kit following manufacturer instructions with some small adjustments (see supplementary methods section: “DNA isolation”). The isolated DNA was measured using the Denovix DS-11, and ranged from 1.7 to 12 ng/µL. Genomic DNA libraries were subsequently prepared using the TruSeq DNA Nano LT Sample Preparation Kit (Illumina), whereby DNA was mechanically fragmented, end-repaired and 3′-adenylated, ligated to indexed adapters, size-selected by bead-ba

[Results]
The Luymes Banks consist of a carbonate platform raised from the ocean floor, up to a depth of 60–80 m below the ocean surface and features multiple sinkholes with depths of up to 475 m below the ocean surface across their 66 km2 area [71]. We performed a characterization of seven of these sinkholes and adjacent open-ocean stations using multivariate clustering of hydrographic and biogeochemical parameters (phosphate, nitrate, nitrite, pH, depth, dissolved oxygen, transmissivity, salinity, and chlorophyll,(Fig. 1B, C). We excluded total alkalinity from the clustering analysis due to its strong collinearity with dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC, Supplementary Fig. S3). The multivariate clustering revealed six distinct environments: surface, platform, shallow sinkhole, deep sinkhole, acid lake, and mesopelagic (Fig. 1 C, D). Each cluster delineates a discrete physicochemical biome characterized by a unique combination of water column properties (Supplementary Fig. S3B), that approximately correspond to increasing depths (surface: n = 16, mean = 2.7 m, std = 3 m; platform: n = 12, mean = 70 m, std = 6 m, shallow sinkhole: n = 14, mean = 92 m, std = 10 m; deep sinkhole: n = 9, mean = 177 m, std = 47 m; acid lake: n = 6, mean = 275 m, std = 30 m; and mesopelagic: n = 2, mean = 536 m, std = 76 m). With the notable exception of the acid lake, the six different environments correspond to regular oceanographic patterns including higher nutrient levels in deeper, cooler water, and a chlorophyll max at intermediate depth [12, 40]. Samples collected near the surface (surface) were similar across all sinkholes and the open ocean, featuring high light, temperature, and dissolved oxygen with low concentrations of salinity, inorganic nutrients, and chlorophyll (Fig. 1C, D, E). Samples collected just above the platform depth at a depth of 60–80 m (platform), had higher salinity (mean = 37 ppt,std = 0.18 ppt) than the surface samples (mean = 34.7 ppt; std = 0.27 ppt), the highest chlorophyll concentrations of all environments (mean = 0.31 µg/kg, std = 0.03 µg/kg), and marginal increases in oxygen (+ 0.3 µmol/kg), nitrate (+ 0.11 µmol/kg), and nitrite (+ 0.035 µmol/kg) relative to the surface. The conditions within the sinkholes (shallow sinkhole, deep sinkhole, and acid lake) diverged from platform waters with increased salinity, nitrate, and phosphate. These patterns were consistent across both northern and southern sinkholes. The most striking deviations from the general p

[Discussion]
Exploring remote habitats has become more accessible thanks to large-scale omics datasets reducing the reliance on laboratory conditions. Yet these environments pose analytical challenges that differ markedly from those encountered in well-characterized or laboratory-controlled systems. A key difficulty lies in the holistic treatment of each sample: all detected metabolites and microbial taxa are jointly associated with the same environmental context, and consequently with one another. This obscures the directionality of causal relationships, as most conclusions are limited to co-occurrences, and our current analysis is primarily correlative. This limitation means that a mechanistic explanation is currently impossible to provide, based on the correlation network alone. Instead, the identified connections should be viewed as hypothesis-generating leads that warrant targeted validation through experiments or modeling. It is also reasonable to expect that aspects of microbial adaptation involve transcriptional changes or protein-level modifications and therefore are not captured in the functional abundance analysis. Further analysis such as protein sequence comparisons or RNA sequencing is likely to reveal additional fascinating insights within this ecosystem, if such data becomes available.
We can contemplate how our results relate to future ocean acidification. Laboratory studies report reduced nitrification rates under acidified conditions [5], yet the acid lake demonstrates that key nitrogen-cycling lineages can persist at pH levels of ~ 6 far below end-century surface ocean projections (~ 7.7–7.8). This suggests that at least some nitrifying archaea and bacteria possess sufficient plasticity to maintain function under chronic acidification. Cyanobacteria, which were still present at a low relative abundance within the nearly aphotic deep sinkholes (mean = 0.03, SD = 0.016), were almost completely lost in the acid lake (mean = 0.0017, SD = 0.0002), suggesting that, even when taking into account the low light conditions, photosynthetic primary producers may be more vulnerable to combined acidification and deoxygenation. Naturally, we should be careful with our interpretations, as the acid lake is nearly aphotic, higher in dissolved inorganic carbon and other nutrients, and resembles a chronically stressed, hydrodynamically isolated endpoint rather than the gradual transition expected in the open ocean,

candidates.title: Dysregulated microbiota-gut-brain axis induced by intermittent access to palatable food is associated with binge-like eating regardless of obesity development.
candidates.abstract: Recurrent consumption of energy dense palatable foods contributes to the rising prevalence of obesity and can also promote loss-of-control eating in a subset of individuals. Obesity is commonly associated with peripheral inflammation, impaired sensitivity to appetite-regulating hormones, and alterations in gut microbiota composition, all of which may exacerbate binge-eating behaviors. However, emerging evidence suggests that repeated exposure to palatable foods alone can induce maladaptive eating patterns even prior to the development of obesity. In this study, intermittent access to palatable food (e.g., cheesecake) induced binge-like eating behavior in non-obese female rats, accompanied by hypothalamic microglial reactivity and altered leptin signaling pathway. Additionally, even sporadic exposure to palatable food was sufficient to alter gut microbiota composition, increasing microbial diversity and promoting taxa adapted to high fat and sugar availability, including potential pathobionts (e.g., Escherichia, Streptococcus, and Clostridium spp.) as well as carbohydrate-fermenting bacteria such as Bifidobacterium and Roseburia . Notably, increased microbial diversity was associated with both hyperphagic behavior and reduced hypothalamic leptin pathway responsiveness. Overall, these findings suggest that gut microbiota imbalance and central neuroimmune adaptations occurred in the absence of significant weight gain. This highlights the potential value of early interventions which may represent promising candidate strategies for future investigation.
candidates.article_body_excerpt:
[Introduction]
Loss-of-control eating, defined as recurrent episodes of binge eating, has long been reported as a pathological eating behavior observed in bulimia nervosa (BN) and binge-eating disorder (BED). 1-4 Compulsive eaters report frequent episodes of consuming large quantities of appetizing foods beyond the satiety threshold, losing control over their eating and experiencing remorse after overeating. Despite somatic and mental aversive consequences, these individuals are unsuccessful in giving up binge eating. 5
Unlike BN, BED does not include compensatory purging actions like vomiting, intense physical activity or excessive dieting, 6 which partially explains its strong association with obesity. Recent evidence suggests that visceral adipose expansion releases fatty acids promoting insulin resistance, increases adipokines such as leptin, and secretes pro-inflammatory cytokines leading to low-grade peripheral inflammation. 7 Hence, abdominal obesity may trigger central inflammation, impair satiety signaling and promote overeating. 8
Meanwhile, multiple studies have reported that autoimmune and inflammatory diseases are associated with increased risk for developing BN and BED, one striking observation being that childhood diagnosis of an autoimmune or autoinflammatory disease increased the risk of developing BN by 73%. 9-11 And although its prevalence clearly increases with excessive weight gain, BED occurs in persons across the weight spectrum, 3 , 12 underscoring the fact that overeating is also reported in the absence of or before the onset of obesity. Preclinical evidence confirms bingeing behaviors in rodents consuming palatable foods weeks before the onset of weight gain, 13 , 14 concomitant with central inflammation 15 and altered gut microbiota composition. 16 , 17 Intermittent binge eating has greater adverse metabolic consequences than the chronic overeating of smaller but more frequent meals, and this chronic binging may compromise immune function. 18 It is well known that central inflammation contributes to overeating by disrupting the signaling cascade of hormones regulating appetite control within hypothalamic regions involved in food intake regulation. 19 The ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) and arcuate nucleus (ARC) play a pivotal role in the integration of homeostatic and hedonic signals driving eating behavior 20 , 21 and increased levels of proinflammatory factors in these brain regions, among which various cytokines including IL-1, IFN-γ, TNF-α 

[Materials and methods]
Thirty-five 6-week-old Wistar Han female rats (weighing 174.11 g ± 3.38 at the beginning of the experiment) were used in this study. The rats were bred in our animal facility from breeding pairs obtained from Charles River Laboratories (France) and were maintained under conventional health conditions. All animals were kept under a 12-h light/dark cycle (light off at 9 am) in temperature- and humidity-controlled room. Food and water were provided ad libitum and all manipulations (animal weighing, change of diet, stool collection) were done during the dark phase of the light cycle. The entire experiment was carried out in agreement with the Swiss Cantonal Veterinary Office and the Committee for animal experimentation (authorization VD3047.1). Animals were monitored daily for body condition, general appearance and signs of pain or distress. No unexpected adverse events occurred during the study. Rats were block-randomized into the C/C and C/P groups by an experimenter blinded to subsequent behavioral outcomes, matched for baseline body weight and food intake. Within each diet group, animals were further randomly and blindly pre-assigned, prior to the start of the intermittent feeding protocol, to one of two terminal-procedure sub-cohorts: (i) decapitation with trunk-blood and fecal collection (used for microbiota, SCFA, serum inflammatory markers, and qPCR gene expression), or (ii) transcardiac perfusion (used for microglial morphology study). These two endpoints are mutually exclusive at the tissue level (perfusion-fixation precludes serum collection and optimal RNA extraction, while decapitation precludes optimal fixation for high-resolution immunohistochemistry). Consequently, these analyses were performed in separate, non-overlapping sub-cohorts of animals rather than using different tissues from the same animals.
No animals were excluded from the study after allocation. Analysis-specific exclusions resulting from unavailable or insufficient samples are reported together with the final sample size for each outcome. Whenever feasible, sample processing, image acquisition, outcome quantification and statistical analysis were performed blindly.
6-week-old rats were individually housed (in type III cages 425 × 266 × 185 mm containing a wooden arch and nesting material as enrichment) and after ten days of acclimatization they were split in two groups of equal food intake: 17 of them were assigned to the control C/C (chow/chow) group and received standard chow 

[Results]
Control C/C rats maintained stable daily intake throughout the eight-week protocol (Figure 2A). In contrast, C/P rats consumed more calories during cheesecake access and less chow after returning to the chow-only phase, with the reduction in chow intake becoming apparent from week 3 (Figure 2B). Over the full protocol, cumulative caloric intake was higher in C/P than in C/C (C/C: 3 141 ± 62 kcal; C/P: 3 363 ± 56.6 kcal; t = 2.643, P = 0.0125), whereas body-weight trajectories did not differ between groups (Figure 2C). The cumulative values shown in Figure 2A and B cover the complete 48-h access period, whereas Figure 2D reports intake during the first 6 h of the first access day.
To assess binge-like eating, food intake was recorded every two hours (from 0 h to 6 h after cheesecake availability) on the first day of cheesecake access during week 1 and week 8. In week 1, both groups ingested a similar proportion of daily calories in the first two-hour interval (C/C: 14.2% ± 6.1%; C/P: 10.3% ± 8.8%). By week 8, C/P rats consumed 28.8% of their daily calories within the first two hours of cheesecake availability, indicative of pronounced binge-like eating compared both to the control group and to their intake during the first week of exposure (Figure 2D), as confirmed by two-way repeated-measures ANOVA (Time × Group: F(5,165) = 10.56, P < 0.0001; Time: F(3.965, 130.8) = 5.3, P = 0.0006; Group: F(1,33) = 8.284, P = 0.007). Intermediate 2-h intake measurements were not collected during weeks 2–7, by design, to minimize handling-related disturbance across the full 8-week protocol; the trajectory of binge-phenotype emergence between week 1 and week 8 therefore cannot be further resolved with the present dataset, and finer-grained temporal sampling is recommended in future studies.
Effect of intermittent feeding protocol on food intake (A–B): (A) Daily food intake of C/C and C/P group during all the experiment. C/P rats show higher energy intake during cheesecake exposure. (B) Food intake of C/C and C/P rats by phase. C/P rats exhibit increased food intake when fed cheesecake and a progressive reduction in food intake when returned to standard chow (C/C n = 17, C/P n = 18; 2-way repeated measure ANOVA followed by Sidak's multiple comparison; *p < 0.05). Effect of intermittent feeding protocol on body weight: (C) body weight of C/C and C/P rats during the entire experiment. No difference in body weight was observed between the two groups. [Discussion]
The microbiota–gut–brain axis has emerged as a promising conceptual framework for understanding binge eating disorder pathophysiology, extending classical models that view eating disorders primarily through psychological or behavioral lenses. 35 , 36 , 74 , 75 This study provides converging evidence that intermittent access to palatable food triggers a sequence of biological changes through complex neuroinflammatory pathways and modified leptin signaling mechanisms, thereby creating a self-perpetuating cycle of disordered eating behavior that occurs independently of body weight changes. These findings provide a basis for generating hypotheses regarding potential therapeutic targets and preventive strategies, although their clinical relevance remains to be established.
Binge-eating behaviors and related eating disorders are substantially more prevalent in females, both in humans and animal models, 76 , 77 supporting a biological basis for sex-specific vulnerability. In addition, sex differences in gut microbiota composition, neuroimmune signaling, and microbiota–brain interactions are increasingly recognized. 78 Hormonal, metabolic, and immune-related differences between sexes may therefore influence microbiota composition, SCFA production, and hypothalamic inflammatory responses. Consequently, the findings reported here in females may not directly generalize to males, and future studies including both sexes will be necessary to evaluate sex-specific microbiota–brain mechanisms involved in binge-eating behavior. Rats were housed individually to accurately measure per-animal food intake, a requirement for the primary behavioral endpoint. Although this may induce chronic stress, its equal application to C/C and C/P groups cannot explain between-group differences.
Our central finding is that brief, intermittent exposure to palatable food (only two consecutive days per week for eight weeks) substantially alters gut bacterial composition and functional products, potentially affecting brain function and feeding behavior. The microbiota shifted consistently, with enrichment of Bifidobacterium, Streptococcus, Roseburia, and Eubacterium alongside depletion of Alistipes and Prevotella. This pattern resembles chronic Western diet-induced remodeling, 79 , 80 suggesting that even brief, intermittent consumption of palatable food can induce microbiological changes. candidates.title: Amino acid-based formula and Clostridioides difficile -associated disease in infants: concerns regarding causal interpretation.
candidates.abstract: Wang et al. recently reported an association between amino acid-based formula (AAF) feeding and Clostridioides difficile -associated disease (CDAD) in children younger than two years, integrating clinical observations, microbiome profiling, and fecal microbiota transplantation experiments. The authors appropriately framed their findings as associative; our aim is not to allege over-interpretation, but to delineate the evidentiary gap between their reported association and a causal claim. Several methodological and interpretative issues limit such inference, including confounding by the clinical indication for AAF, the difficulty of distinguishing C. difficile colonization from clinically attributable disease in young children, developmental differences in age and complementary feeding, and the selected nature of the fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) donor population. For example, the multivariable model included only 27 outcome events against approximately six predictors (events-per-variable ≈ 4.5, far below the accepted 10-20 threshold), rendering the adjusted odds ratios unstable. The cross-sectional microbiome data further cannot establish whether microbial alterations preceded disease or resulted from underlying clinical, dietary, or inflammatory states. We therefore suggest interpreting the findings as an association between AAF feeding and CDAD status, rather than evidence that AAF itself increases CDAD risk. Our skepticism concerns the causal link to CDAD specifically; we do not dispute that reduced Bifidobacterium with formula feeding is a well-established finding. This distinction has important clinical implications, as AAF remains an essential nutritional intervention for children with appropriate indications, and in young children microbiological detection and microbiome alterations must be interpreted alongside age, clinical symptoms, underlying disease, dietary history, and other relevant exposures. An overly causal interpretation could create unnecessary concern among families and complicate clinical decision-making. To make these considerations operational, we specify the elements of a decisive prospective study, including a minimum event count of ~60 adjudicated CDAD cases, a blinded tiered diagnostic algorithm, and detailed AAF exposure ascertainment.
candidates.article_body_excerpt:
[Introduction]
Wang and colleagues recently published a study in Gut Microbes (2026;18:2719259) reporting a significant association between amino acid-based formula (AAF) feeding and increased risk of Clostridioides difficile-associated disease (CDAD) in children under two years of age. 1 The study addresses an important and understudied clinical question and combines clinical observations, microbiome profiling, and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) experiments. The authors identified a robust association between AAF exposure and CDAD incidence; moreover, they demonstrated markedly reduced Bifidobacterium abundance in AAF-fed infants and increased susceptibility to C. difficile infection (CDI) in PEG-conditioned mice colonized with microbiota derived from AAF-fed infants.
At the outset, we note that Wang et al. framed their findings as associative, acknowledged that confounding by indication could not be excluded, and appropriately called for larger prospective studies. We also do not dispute their microbiome observations: reduced Bifidobacterium with formula feeding relative to breastfeeding is among the most replicated findings in infant gut microbiology. Our aim in this commentary is therefore not to allege over-interpretation by the original authors, but to delineate the evidentiary gap between their reported association and a causal claim, and to specify what additional evidence would close it. This distinction matters because several features of the study, while compatible with the authors' cautious framing, could be read by clinicians and families as establishing causation. A concrete example illustrates the gap: the multivariable analysis rests on 27 outcome events distributed across approximately six dietary predictors, an events-per-variable ratio of ~4.5 that is far below accepted thresholds, so the adjusted effect estimates carry considerable uncertainty.
Nevertheless, several methodological and interpretative considerations warrant attention when translating these findings into causal and clinical conclusions. In particular, confounding by the clinical indication for AAF, the difficulty of distinguishing C. difficile colonization from clinically attributable disease in young children, 2 , 3 the developmental context of infant feeding, 4 , 5 and the selected nature of the experimental FMT model may limit causal inference. We discuss these issues below and consider their implications for interpreting AAF-associated CDAD risk.

[Discussion]
AAF is not a randomly assigned exposure. According to ESPGHAN and Chinese Society of Pediatrics guidelines, AAF is indicated for dietary replacement during the diagnostic period of suspected cow's milk protein allergy (CMPA), severe CMPA, multiple food allergies, or related clinical indications. 6 , 7 These underlying conditions may themselves influence intestinal inflammation, mucosal function, dietary patterns, and gut microbial composition. Previous studies have also reported alterations in the gut microbiota, including reduced Bifidobacterium, in infants with CMPA. 8–10
The authors acknowledge that confounding by indication cannot be entirely ruled out. However, adjustment for a binary history of food allergy may not fully capture the clinical heterogeneity underlying AAF prescription. Disease severity, gastrointestinal symptoms preceding AAF initiation, duration of AAF exposure, elimination diets, prior formula intolerance, and the timing of AAF initiation may all influence the observed microbial phenotype. 11 Moreover, because AAF is available in China without prescription and is used by some parents for dyspeptic symptoms outside strict CMPA indications (a caveat Wang et al. themselves raised), the exposed population mixes true CMPA with a broader symptomatic population, making a single binary covariate even less adequate.
That potential confounders are difficult to eliminate by simple adjustment for a binary variable is a well-established methodological principle. Confounding by indication is a recognized source of spurious association in observational research, and single-covariate adjustment does not recover causal effects when the confounder is multi-dimensional (e.g., disease severity, healthcare utilization). 11 Better-suited approaches include indication-stratified analyses, propensity-score weighting or matching constructed from the full pre-AAF clinical phenotype, 12 , 13 and, most powerfully, within-child designs in which each patient serves as their own control. An instrumental-variable approach, for example exploiting regional variation in prescribing practice, offers a further option, although its identifying assumptions would be difficult to verify in a study of this size. We also recognize that the original study's modest sample size precludes most of these methods, which is itself a reason the association should not yet be read causally.

[Conclusions]
We appreciate the authors' efforts in addressing this clinically important question, and our comments are intended to refine the interpretation of their valuable findings rather than to challenge their observations, a goal aligned with the authors' own appropriately cautious framing. Wang et al. have identified an association between AAF feeding and CDAD that warrants further investigation, but the current evidence does not establish causality, and the dimensions of the analysis (27 events across ~6 predictors) mean the adjusted estimates should be treated as hypothesis-generating.
Clinically, the stakes of this distinction are concrete: in young children, C. difficile detection may coexist with asymptomatic colonization, and gastrointestinal symptoms may have multiple causes. Interpreting microbiological findings in isolation, particularly in children receiving AAF for underlying allergic or gastrointestinal conditions, risks creating unnecessary concern and complicating clinical decisions. The present study should stimulate the prospective, adequately powered, carefully adjudicated investigations we have outlined, not discourage or delay AAF use when clinically warranted.

candidates.title: Mapping the genetic landscape of microbial lipid transformation in the intestinal microbiome.
candidates.abstract: Dietary lipids are a key component in our diet, and fats and their derivatives have been associated with both beneficial as well as adverse effects on host health. However, the contribution of the gut microbiome to lipid metabolism remains understudied. Recognizing the importance of this interplay, we conducted extensive literature reviews to identify key bacterial genes involved in lipid metabolism, and created 88 Hidden Markov Models to allow rapid and accurate identification of these genes in genome and metagenome data. We applied these models to over 1000 metagenomes representative of the small intestine and colon, from both population-based and disease cohorts (LLDeep, MetaCardis and 1000IBD) to determine their lipolytic capacity. We observed that microbiome community types (enterotypes) carry different lipolytic potential. Serum levels of conjugated and sulfonated secondary bile acids were significantly associated with increased abundance of sterol-sulfonation genes ( cysC, cysD and BtSULT ). Small-intestinal communities were enriched in lipid genes compared to the colonic microbiota, underscoring the importance of microbial lipid metabolism in the small intestine compared to the colon. Overall, we demonstrate the value of our lipid metabolism models for functional microbiome profiling. Additionally, our study suggests that microbial activity in the upper gut might play a direct role in shaping host lipid metabolism, with potential implications for cardiometabolic health.
candidates.article_body_excerpt:
[Introduction]
The important role of the gut microbiome in mediating the effects of diet on host health is well established. 1 However, scientific efforts have been biased towards carbohydrate and protein metabolism, to date. This emphasis is reflected in one of the most widely used algorithms and frameworks for annotating metabolic functions in metagenomic data, the human gut metabolic modules (GMMs). 2 Of the 103 modules (version 1.07), more than half are dedicated to saccharolytic functions, 39 modules are dedicated to proteolytic functions and only 11 modules are dedicated to lipolytic or lipid-associated functions. Although several tools exist to comprehensively profile carbohydrate metabolism in the gut microbiome, the community's capacity for lipid metabolism remains largely uncharacterized. 3 , 4 The underrepresentation of lipid metabolism is significant given the important role lipids play in human health. 5
Dietary lipids are predominantly triglycerides (TAGs), accounting for 90% of our total lipid intake. TAGs are composed of a glycerol backbone esterified to three long chain fatty acids (LCFA). The remaining dietary lipids consist of sterols, phospholipids, glycerolipids and fat-soluble vitamins. 6 A small fraction of phospholipids has a hydrophilic residue (e.g., choline) attached to their glycerol backbone, while sterols represent the smallest lipid fraction 7 Fats and their derivatives have been associated with both beneficial and adverse effects on host health, and current dietary recommendations state that up to 40% of our daily energy intake should be derived from beneficial fatty acids. 6 , 7 Lipids with beneficial health effects are mostly TAGs containing unsaturated fatty acids, such as linoleic acid, and have been linked to improved cardiovascular health and inflammation reduction. 8-11 Conversely, certain lipid classes, including saturated fatty acids, as well as lipid-derived compounds such as choline, have been implicated in negative effects on cardiovascular health and weight regulation. 12-14
In the upper intestinal tract, host and bacterial derived lipases break down these complex dietary lipids into their constituent components; glycerol, free fatty acids and, when applicable, headgroups. Microorganisms possess the functional capacity to metabolize these breakdown products, rather than the intact lipid molecules. 15 Recent studies have shown that changes in dietary lipid intake can rapidly and profoundly reshape the composition and metabolic 

[Results]
Based on an extensive literature review, we created and curated a comprehensive set of Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) specifically designed to detect microbial genes within metagenomes which contribute to the metabolic capacity for dietary-lipid conversions (Supplemental Table S1). Experimentally validated gene genes were selected as seed sequences for the HMM construction. Reference organisms included both known inhabitants of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract as well as species associated with lipid metabolization isolated from other niches (Supplemental Table S2), 23 enabling the detection of both established and potentially overlooked lipid conversions genes in gut microbial communities.
For clarity, these predicted lipid-related protein functions are hereafter referred to as lipid genes and refer to genes with direct or accessory functions in lipid metabolism. The HMMs covered both lipid-specific genes (involved exclusively in lipid metabolism or conversion) and accessory genes (associated with, but not limited to, the conversion of lipids and their derivatives). The lipid-specific transformations were subdivided into fatty acid transformation (with a focus on linoleic acid), β-oxidation, sterol transformation and degradation, choline degradation, sphingolipid and phospholipid modification, and membrane transportation. The accessory categories were added as TAG degradation produces glycerol 24 , 25 and long chain fatty acids. Both glycerol and fatty acids are highly reduced substrates, and their oxidation generates reducing equivalents that must be transferred to electron acceptors to maintain cellular redox balance. 26 , 27 Consequently, we included genes involved in electron transfer and energy conservation (e.g., nuo and nqr) as well as glycerol conversion and degradation as accessory functions that may support the utilization of lipid-derived substrates, while acknowledging that these genes are not specific to lipid metabolism. Additionally, we incorporated key genes for the synthesis of vitamin K and B2, as these two vitamins have been associated with lipids. 28 , 29 In total, we identified 88 key genes (Supplemental Table S1) associated with lipid transformation.
To evaluate the functional specificity of the resulting HMMs, all seed proteins were analyzed with InterPro 30 (Supplemental Table S3, Figure S1). Functional predictions from the integrated NCBIfam, Pfam, PANTHER, HAMAP, and other InterPro member databases were highly consistent with the exp

[Discussion]
Our modelling framework captures a broader repertoire of lipid‑associated functions, including 42 genes involved in the transformation of lipid‑derived compounds such as fatty acids and choline, thereby providing a more comprehensive representation of the dietary lipid‑modifying potential of the gut microbiome. It encompasses lipid transformations with potential health implications, including conversions of bioactive lipid metabolites such as linoleic acid derivatives. By integrating lipid-specific and accessory functions alongside vitamin biosynthesis linked to lipid metabolism, this resource enables a more holistic assessment of the interactions between lipids and their derivatives, the microbiome and their collective impact on human health.
In line with the need to expand lipid‑centric microbiome models, we examined how enterotype stratification shapes the distribution of lipid‑associated functions across the gut microbiome. We found that stratifying the BMIS dataset 21 by enterotype explained the majority of the variance in lipid gene abundance. Notably, the two Bacteroides enterotypes remained those with the highest inferred lipolytic potential, in agreement with prior findings. 2 , 21 Among these, Bacteroides 2 exhibited the highest number of unique lipid‑associated functions when normalized by total functional diversity. Interestingly, Bacteroides enterotypes have been associated with more Western-style diets, rich in protein and (saturated) fats. 44 , 45 One contributing factor may be the relatively higher abundance of Escherichia species in the Bacteroides 2 enterotype, 21 a species with a versatile lipolytic capacity (this study 21 ). Alternatively, the enrichment of lipid‑associated functions in this enterotype may reflect a relatively greater contribution from small‑intestinal microbes compared with colonic inhabitants. This shift may be driven by the lower overall microbial load characteristic of this enterotype, 32 , 46 which could increase the proportional representation of DNA originating from small‑intestinal communities in stool samples. Such a compositional bias may partially explain the distinctive lipid‑related functional repertoire observed for this enterotype.
Among the genes enriched in the Bacteroides 2 enterotype, steroidal metabolite sulfonation genes (BtSULT, cysC, and cysD) were particularly notable in the context of host health. These genes have been reported to modulate the sulfation of cholesterol and bile acids, with downst

[Limitations]
Our analysis considered both colonic as well as small intestine communities, however, we were limited in small intestine community datasets availability. The small intestine dataset used in our study was of participants with an ileostomy or ileoanal pouch, who although reported healthy, have a small intestine community which can differ from people without an ileostomy or ileoanal pouch. While stoma effluent represents the most effective method for studying the small intestine at large-scale and with high resolution, two important limitations must be acknowledged: the underlying disease history of the participants and the inability to capture physiological and microbial differences across different sections of the small intestine. Future studies using advanced sampling methods, such as endoscopic pills, may help expand and validate our findings in healthy individuals and further explore the diversity of microbial lipid metabolism across the small intestine. Although sampling, sequencing and bioinformatic processing was harmonized across cohorts, residual cohort-specific batch effects cannot be excluded. Because the overlap between location and cohort conventional batch-correction approaches could not be applied. However, small intestine microbial compositions in our cohort aligns with previously reported compositions, suggesting that any potential remaining batch effect should be minimal. This reflects the limited availability of high-quality metagenomes from regular small intestinal communities, obtained without ileostomy or ileoanal pouch, but by catheter or ingestible pills. Consequently the resolution at which their contributions to host health can be assessed remains limited. Another limitation was that for many of the genes we now assign functions to have not been functionally characterized in a gut context with biochemical assays or similar. Extensive evaluation of lipid gene function in vitro using gut-representing species and strains and/or heterologous expression platforms would be needed to strengthen the function assignments used. We base our findings on gene richness and abundance comparisons, while gene expression levels are likely more relevant to predict the lipid-modifying activity levels.
